narrative:
The model estimated a 72.8% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the school treated that high-risk prediction as decisive, your application was rejected. This does not mean you cannot succeed; it means your file closely resembled patterns the model associated with first-time bar failure.

The strongest factor was your Year 3 class standing: you were in the lowest decile, compared with an accepted-student average around the sixth decile. That very low relative standing pushed the prediction most strongly toward failure. The second most important factor was your LSAT score of 23.5, well below the accepted-student average of about 37.2; this also pushed toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.60, below the accepted average of 3.23, was the third most important factor, but it was the only top-three factor that leaned toward passing rather than failing. It was not enough to offset the concerns about your Year 3 standing and LSAT.

Next, ask admissions whether an appeal, reconsideration, or conditional pathway exists. Provide context for your Year 3 performance, and ask what evidence would strengthen a future application. Consider retaking the LSAT and completing additional coursework or advising that demonstrates readiness for law study and bar preparation.
